title: Northstar AI - Technical deep dive (routing + fallback) after standard demo
summary: SE-led deep dive focused on how Redwood routing policies and fallback behave under capacity constraints, latency SLOs, and regional/data residency requirements. Northstar clarified they need deterministic-ish behavior for evaluation, guardrails to avoid surprise model changes, and a defined error/timeout policy for their production traffic. Redwood walked through route composition (primary + compatible fallback variants), health signals used for routing, and what is and isn’t automatic today (e.g., fallback on 5xx/timeout vs semantic quality). Group aligned on a 2-week POC plan: replay a sanitized traffic sample, set SLO targets, define a failover matrix, and validate observability dashboards + alerting in a dedicated tenant with pinned versions.
topics: Routing policies: latency vs cost vs region
Model/version pinning + update policy for demos vs POC
Observability: per-route latency, token cost, errors, fallback rate
POC scope, success criteria, and timeline
questions: Can we guarantee the model never changes without our approval (including quantization/profile changes)?
What exactly triggers a fallback (429, 5xx, latency budget exceeded, queue depth)?
Can fallback be cross-region, and how do we enforce EU-only for some traffic?
How do we measure and cap the quality regression if we fall back to a smaller model?
Can we do canary routing by header or user cohort and roll back automatically?
next_steps: Redwood to share a proposed fallback matrix (primary + compatible fallbacks) for Northstar’s top 2 workloads (chat + extraction).
Northstar to provide a sanitized request log sample (prompt templates + typical max tokens) and target SLOs per endpoint.
Redwood to provision a POC tenant with pinned model versions, two routes (cost-optimized and latency-optimized), and prebuilt dashboards.
Schedule a 45-min POC kickoff to finalize acceptance criteria and security requirements (retention/logging, IP allowlist/SSO).
action_items: Markus Klein - Send POC plan one-pager (timeline, success criteria, roles) to Dana by 2025-01-17
Mina Haddad - Draft routing + fallback configuration proposal (including triggers and thresholds) by 2025-01-20
Colin O'Donnell - Confirm whether Northstar needs EU-only routing in POC and what regions to enable by 2025-01-20
Dana Wu - Deliver sanitized traffic sample + endpoint definitions (latency targets, throughput) by 2025-01-21
Sofia Ramirez - Share current alert thresholds / incident policy for LLM endpoint errors (5xx/timeout) by 2025-01-21
transcript:
Fireflies.ai Transcript

Title: Northstar AI - Technical deep dive (routing + fallback) after standard demo
Recorded: 2025-01-16 21:00 UTC
Duration: 58 minutes

Attendees
- Markus Klein (Redwood Inference) - Solutions Engineering
- Mina Haddad (Redwood Inference) - Routing/Fallback Lead
- Colin O'Donnell (Redwood Inference) - Demo Integrations
- Dana Wu (Northstar AI) - Director of Platform Engineering
- Arjun Mehta (Northstar AI) - Staff ML Engineer
- Sofia Ramirez (Northstar AI) - SRE


[00:00] Markus Klein: Cool. Okay, thanks everyone for hopping back on after the demo. This one is meant to be like, deeper routing and fallback, because that’s the part you asked the most questions on.

[00:11] Dana Wu: Yeah. The demo was helpful, but we need to understand what is deterministic versus, you know, “magic.”

[00:18] Markus Klein: Totally fair. And Mina is here, she owns a bunch of the routing layer.

[00:22] Mina Haddad: Hey everyone.

[00:23] Arjun Mehta: Hi.

[00:25] Sofia Ramirez: Hello.

[00:27] Markus Klein: Maybe Dana, can you restate what you’re trying to achieve? Like what problem routing/fallback is solving on your side.

[00:35] Dana Wu: Sure. We have two main endpoints. One is a chat endpoint for internal analyst workflows. The other is structured extraction, like JSON output, that feeds downstream systems. We can tolerate some degradation on chat, but extraction can’t silently get weird. And we also have this requirement: if the model is unavailable, we prefer partial functionality over outage, but we need to control *which* fallback happens.

[01:02] Markus Klein: That makes sense.

[01:04] Dana Wu: And we had issues with vendors where fallback happens and nobody knows, then suddenly outputs shift, and our evals go red.

[01:13] Mina Haddad: Yep. So we should separate two concepts: (1) model selection / routing policy, and (2) fallback behavior when the chosen target can’t serve within constraints.

[01:24] Arjun Mehta: Constraints meaning latency, or like capacity?

[01:27] Mina Haddad: Both. In Redwood we treat it as a set of signals: hard errors (5xx), timeouts, rate limiting / admission control, and optionally latency budget. But the key is: you can configure which signals trigger fallback, and you can require explicit compatibility.

[01:46] Markus Klein: And to be clear, “compatibility” is not us guessing. It’s your configured list. So route A can fall back to model B and C, but not to, like, whatever is cheapest.

[01:58] Dana Wu: Okay. So if we pin a model version, we can also pin the fallback versions?

[02:02] Mina Haddad: Yes. We support version pinning at the route target level. So you can pin: primary is, say, model X version 2025-01-10, quant profile Q4_KM, and fallback is model X smaller variant version 2025-01-07, or whatever your matrix is.

[02:20] Sofia Ramirez: And what about regions? We have some EU-only workloads.

[02:23] Mina Haddad: Regions are a routing constraint too. You can set “allowed regions” on the route, and then fallback respects that constraint. So if EU-only, we will not fall back to US even if EU is degraded, unless you explicitly allow cross-region.

[02:39] Sofia Ramirez: Good, because we got burned on that previously.

[02:42] Markus Klein: Yeah, and this is one of those things we want to make very explicit in the demo tenant, and even more in a POC tenant.

[02:49] Arjun Mehta: On triggers: if you have a 429 from quotas, does that trigger fallback or just fail?

[02:56] Mina Haddad: Great question. By default, 429 indicates you’ve hit a configured rate limit or concurrency cap. Most customers don’t want fallback on 429 because it can amplify load and cost. But we can set it either way. Typically we do: 429 returns to caller, and you implement retry/backoff. Or if you want, we can do “soft admission” where we queue within a small window then either serve or fail.

[03:22] Markus Klein: For demos we usually avoid fallback on 429 because it makes behavior confusing. For POC we can set exactly what you want.

[03:30] Dana Wu: I think for us, if it’s a per-tenant quota issue, fallback doesn’t help. If it’s capacity on the backend, then fallback does help.

[03:39] Mina Haddad: Exactly. So we’d separate “tenant quota throttles” from “backend saturation.” Backend saturation we detect via health and queue depth; that can trigger fallback.

[03:52] Sofia Ramirez: Can you define health? Like is it Kubernetes readiness, or actual model latency?

[03:58] Mina Haddad: It’s a combination. There’s infrastructure health (instance up, GPU visible, etc.), and serving health (error rate, tail latency, queue depth). We don’t do anything fancy like semantic health, but we *do* have per-route telemetry and we can trip circuit breakers.

[04:19] Arjun Mehta: Circuit breaker meaning you stop sending traffic to primary?

[04:22] Mina Haddad: Yes. For a period. And optionally you can require N consecutive bad windows.

[04:30] Markus Klein: And we surface that in Console, so you can see “primary unhealthy → fallback activated” with timestamps.

[04:37] Dana Wu: During the demo, you showed a “fallback rate” panel. Is that per route or global?

[04:42] Colin O'Donnell: In the standard demo dashboards, it’s per route, plus a tenant rollup. For POC we can make it per endpoint or header too.

[04:50] Sofia Ramirez: Header-based routing is important. We can mark traffic from canary users.

[04:55] Mina Haddad: Yep. We support routing by request attributes. Most common: API key, header, or a “policy tag.” That’s how we do canaries and A/B.

[05:07] Arjun Mehta: Okay, but say we route canary to primary model version V2 and the rest to V1. If V2 breaks, can you auto rollback?

[05:16] Mina Haddad: Auto rollback can be configured on error/latency SLO breach. But I want to be careful: it’s deterministic based on metrics, not on output quality.

[05:27] Markus Klein: For output quality, we usually pair it with evals or guardrails you run, then you flip the route.

[05:34] Dana Wu: Right, because quality is a different signal.

[05:38] Arjun Mehta: On extraction, we require JSON. The demo had structured output. If fallback happens to a smaller model, JSON validity might drop.

[05:48] Mina Haddad: That’s where the compatibility list matters. You can pick fallback models that you’ve validated on JSON schema adherence. Also, we can add response validation at the gateway level—like “must parse as JSON.” But if it fails, you need to decide: do we retry, do we fall back again, or do we fail fast.

[06:10] Sofia Ramirez: Is that in product today, or more like roadmap?

[06:13] Markus Klein: Light validation is in the gateway. Full semantic validation, no. But for POC we can implement a simple “JSON parse + required keys” check and then take action.

[06:25] Arjun Mehta: If it fails, could you route to a safer but slower model, like a bigger one?

[06:30] Mina Haddad: Yes, that’s actually a common pattern: latency-optimized primary, then “quality fallback” second, but only on validation failure. We just need to be explicit, because you don’t want infinite loops.

[06:44] Dana Wu: That would be nice. We also want a max cost guardrail.

[06:48] Markus Klein: Yep. You can cap max output tokens per request, and you can also set cost budgets per route, but those are usually more for reporting and alerts than hard enforcement. For hard enforcement we do token limits and quotas.

[07:04] Sofia Ramirez: On timeouts: what do you consider a timeout? Client-side? Server-side?

[07:08] Mina Haddad: Both exist. The serving runtime has a per-request deadline. The gateway also enforces request timeouts. And then you can set a “fallback deadline,” like: if we haven’t started streaming within X ms, try fallback.

[07:25] Arjun Mehta: Wait, fallback after streaming starts would be weird.

[07:28] Mina Haddad: We don’t do that. Once streaming begins, we stick with the chosen backend.

[07:34] Markus Klein: Otherwise you’d get half a response from one model and then another, which would be… not good.

[07:39] Dana Wu: Good.

[07:41] Sofia Ramirez: What about long generations. If we hit a backend issue mid-stream, what happens?

[07:48] Mina Haddad: Typically the connection drops. We log it. We can support resumable patterns with client retry using a request id, but full “resume token generation” depends on KV cache persistence. Not something I want to promise as automatic.

[08:06] Markus Klein: The safe pattern is: if streaming disconnect, your app retries from last known state or re-asks. For demos we have a Plan B script that switches to non-streaming if the network is flaky.

[08:18] Dana Wu: Makes sense.

[08:20] Markus Klein: Let’s talk about what you’d need to feel comfortable: what are your SLOs? Like p95 latency and error budgets.

[08:28] Dana Wu: For chat, p95 under 2 seconds to first token, and p99 maybe 5 seconds. For extraction, we can tolerate 6 to 8 seconds but errors must be extremely low, like under 0.1% 5xx.

[08:44] Sofia Ramirez: And we want a clear incident mode: if primary is down, we’d rather degrade but still return something, with alerting so we know.

[08:54] Markus Klein: Perfect. That maps directly to routing policy + alerts: fallback rate > X%, 5xx > Y%, first-token latency > Z.

[09:06] Arjun Mehta: Can you show what information we get when fallback happens? Like in logs.

[09:12] Colin O'Donnell: In Console you see per-request tracing if enabled, but in standard mode you’ll get request id, route name, selected target, whether it was fallback, and why (e.g., “primary_unhealthy” or “deadline_exceeded”). We can also export to your SIEM if you have that set up, but for POC we usually just use the built-in logs.

[09:37] Sofia Ramirez: We would need at least log export eventually. We use Datadog today.

[09:41] Markus Klein: Cool. For POC, we can do the built-in dashboards plus a webhook export or just CSV. But long-term we have integrations.

[09:50] Mina Haddad: One nuance: sometimes people say “fallback” but they mean “load balancing.” In Redwood, within a target pool, we balance across replicas. Fallback is crossing from one target definition to a different one.

[10:05] Arjun Mehta: Like from model A to model B.

[10:07] Mina Haddad: Exactly. Or from quant profile Q4 to Q8, if you choose to define that.

[10:14] Dana Wu: Quant profile switching without approval is a no-go for us.

[10:18] Markus Klein: 100%. In a POC tenant we will pin everything and updates happen only on your approval.

[10:25] Arjun Mehta: How do you handle “silent updates” in hosted generally? Like if you roll a new kernel.

[10:32] Mina Haddad: Kernel-level updates can happen, yes, but the model artifact version remains pinned. If your concern is output drift, kernel changes usually shouldn’t change output, but performance might change slightly. For absolute control we recommend Dedicated or Private, but even in Hosted we can isolate a POC tenant and keep it stable for the duration.

[10:56] Dana Wu: Okay.

[10:58] Markus Klein: Maybe let’s outline a POC plan that tests the stuff you care about: correctness under fallback, and SLO under load.

[11:07] Sofia Ramirez: Also, our traffic is spiky. We do like 10x bursts.

[11:11] Markus Klein: Got it.

[11:12] Mina Haddad: Then we’ll want to test both admission control behavior and fallback behavior. Otherwise you might think fallback is “fixing” a burst, but it’s actually just pushing cost.

[11:24] Arjun Mehta: Yes. We need predictable spend.

[11:27] Markus Klein: So proposal: 2-week POC. Week 1: integrate, define routes, replay sample traffic, tune batching/caching. Week 2: load test with burst profile, validate dashboards, test failure modes.

[11:43] Dana Wu: What do you need from us to start?

[11:46] Markus Klein: A sanitized traffic sample, or at least prompt templates and typical token ranges. Also your target SLOs. And for fallback matrix, we’ll suggest based on your constraints, but you need to approve which models are acceptable.

[12:03] Arjun Mehta: On “acceptable models,” do you have recommended pairs? Like same family smaller variant.

[12:09] Mina Haddad: Yes, typically we keep within the same model family for behavioral similarity. For example, “70B → 8B” is a bigger jump than “70B → 34B,” but cost-wise maybe you prefer that. We’ll give options and you validate with evals.

[12:26] Sofia Ramirez: And how do we test fallback without taking down prod?

[12:29] Mina Haddad: In the tenant we can simulate failures. We can mark primary unhealthy, or temporarily set the target to 0 capacity, or inject latency. There’s a safe “test mode” route that mirrors traffic.

[12:44] Markus Klein: And we’ll do it in POC tenant, not your prod.

[12:48] Dana Wu: Good.

[12:50] Arjun Mehta: What about “quality monitoring.” You mentioned evals in the demo deck. Is that integrated with routing decisions?

[12:57] Markus Klein: Not directly. Redwood Optimize can run evals on prompt sets and alert on regressions. But routing is operational signals. The typical workflow: you run evals before you change routing, and you can canary.

[13:13] Arjun Mehta: Okay.

[13:15] Sofia Ramirez: So if we have a fallback event, we’ll know via metrics, but we won’t automatically know outputs got worse.

[13:21] Markus Klein: Correct. But we can also log fallback occurrences and you can sample those responses for offline evaluation.

[13:30] Mina Haddad: Some customers also choose to only allow fallback on chat, and fail extraction if primary is down, because silent quality regression is worse than an error.

[13:41] Dana Wu: That’s interesting. For extraction, I might prefer a controlled degrade with explicit flag.

[13:47] Markus Klein: We can add a response header like “X-Redwood-Fallback: true” so your app can decide to treat it differently.

[13:56] Sofia Ramirez: That would help.

[14:00] Arjun Mehta: For our downstream pipeline, we can accept “fallback true” and route to a human review queue.

[14:05] Dana Wu: Exactly.

[14:07] Mina Haddad: Great. That’s a classic pattern.

[14:10] Markus Klein: Let’s talk deployment modes briefly. You’re currently thinking Hosted first, right?

[14:16] Dana Wu: Maybe. Long-term, security might force VPC. But we want to validate value first.

[14:23] Markus Klein: So POC can be Hosted in an isolated tenant with pinned config. If it goes well, step 2 is Dedicated or Private. Routing concepts are the same.

[14:35] Sofia Ramirez: In VPC mode, do we lose any routing features?

[14:38] Mina Haddad: Not functionally. The control plane differs, but routing policies, fallback, dashboards—same product surface.

[14:47] Arjun Mehta: Okay.

[14:49] Markus Klein: One more thing: you mentioned you’ve used Bedrock and Azure OpenAI. What did you like or dislike about their failover?

[14:57] Dana Wu: Bedrock is okay but opaque. You don’t really know what’s happening. Azure gives you region options but again, not a lot of control. We also tried self-hosting vLLM and it was a lot of work just keeping it stable.

[15:13] Sofia Ramirez: Yeah, oncall burden was high.

[15:15] Markus Klein: Totally. Our pitch is: keep control but not DIY the entire stack.

[15:21] Mina Haddad: And also make fallback observable. Like if fallback activates, it should show up as a first-class metric, not hidden.

[15:30] Arjun Mehta: That’s a big deal for us.

[15:33] Markus Klein: Great. Let’s outline the exact artifacts we’ll deliver for POC.

[15:39] Colin O'Donnell: I can set up the tenant config skeleton: routes, quotas, dashboards. Then Mina can fill in the routing policy specifics.

[15:48] Markus Klein: And I’ll send a one-pager with timeline and who does what.

[15:54] Dana Wu: Perfect.

[15:56] Sofia Ramirez: Can you also include alert thresholds you recommend for the demo environment? We’re trying to mirror prod ops.

[16:03] Markus Klein: Yes. We have a standard set: p95 first token, p99 end-to-end, 5xx, 429, fallback rate, and queue depth. We’ll tailor it.

[16:16] Mina Haddad: And we can set alerting to business-hours paging for POC, if you want, so it’s not noisy.

[16:24] Sofia Ramirez: Business hours is fine.

[16:26] Arjun Mehta: Another concern: what happens if primary has “slow but not dead” performance? Like p99 blows up but it’s still returning.

[16:36] Mina Haddad: That’s where latency-based fallback comes in. You can define a latency budget and if the predicted queue time exceeds it, we route to fallback. But it can cause oscillation if not tuned.

[16:51] Arjun Mehta: Oscillation meaning flip-flopping.

[16:53] Mina Haddad: Exactly.

[16:55] Markus Klein: In POC we can test both: strict “only fallback on hard errors” vs “fallback on latency.” Many enterprise teams start with hard errors only.

[17:05] Dana Wu: I’d prefer conservative first.

[17:08] Sofia Ramirez: Same.

[17:10] Markus Klein: Great.

[17:12] Arjun Mehta: For canaries, you said header-based. Could we do a 5% split random?

[17:17] Mina Haddad: Yes, weighted routing. Or deterministic hashing on user id.

[17:23] Arjun Mehta: Deterministic hashing is better.

[17:26] Mina Haddad: Agreed. We can do that.

[17:30] Markus Klein: Cool. We’re at like 18 minutes. Let’s make sure we capture everything and then we’ll do next steps.

[17:37] Dana Wu: One more: can you guarantee that fallback doesn’t change the API response format? Like tool calls.

[17:43] Markus Klein: The API surface is consistent. Tool calling and structured output are supported by the route configuration. But the model’s behavior can vary, which is why we validate models for those capabilities.

[17:57] Mina Haddad: And we’ll ensure the fallback model is certified for the same features you’re using.

[18:03] Dana Wu: Okay.

[18:04] Sofia Ramirez: On observability, do you show “why fallback happened”? That’s key.

[18:10] Colin O'Donnell: Yes, there’s a “fallback reason” dimension. Sometimes transcription calls it “failover cause.” You’ll see categories like “target_unhealthy,” “deadline_exceeded,” “capacity_exhausted.”

[18:27] Sofia Ramirez: Great.

[18:29] Markus Klein: Alright. Let’s shift into POC planning.

[18:33] Markus Klein: Week 1 deliverables on our side: provision tenant; set up two routes—one latency optimized for chat, one quality oriented for extraction; pin versions; configure conservative fallback (hard errors only); dashboards imported.

[18:52] Dana Wu: And our week 1 is integration and traffic sample?

[18:56] Markus Klein: Exactly. You can use our SDK or just curl. Colin has scripts from the demo tenant we can adapt.

[19:05] Colin O'Donnell: Yep. We can provide a small harness that replays a JSONL file and captures responses with request ids.

[19:13] Arjun Mehta: That would be helpful.

[19:15] Markus Klein: Week 2: do load test with burst profile, test failure injection, and verify alerts.

[19:24] Sofia Ramirez: What’s “failure injection” in practice?

[19:27] Mina Haddad: We can temporarily scale primary to zero, or flip health to unhealthy, or introduce artificial sleep to push timeouts. We’ll coordinate so you can watch dashboards as it happens.

[19:42] Sofia Ramirez: Nice.

[19:44] Dana Wu: Success criteria: for chat, keep p95 within the target during normal load. During injected failure, error rate stays low and fallback activates, and we can detect it.

[19:57] Markus Klein: Exactly.

[19:59] Dana Wu: For extraction, I want either a controlled failure with explicit flag or a validated fallback. We can decide after we run evals.

[20:08] Markus Klein: Great. We can start with explicit flag and optional fallback, then iterate.

[20:14] Arjun Mehta: Do you have a recommended “fallback rate” acceptable threshold? Like if it’s >1% it’s bad.

[20:22] Mina Haddad: It depends. For production we usually aim for <0.1% sustained fallback. But in POC you might see more because we’re testing. More important is: fallback isn’t hiding issues.

[20:37] Sofia Ramirez: Agreed.

[20:40] Markus Klein: Okay, last five-ish minutes, we’ll recap next steps.

[20:46] Dana Wu: Actually one last question: in the demo you mentioned “smart routing by cost.” Is that dynamic? Like spot pricing.

[20:53] Markus Klein: It’s policy-driven. We don’t do real-time spot auction routing. It’s more: you choose a cost-optimized route which uses a cheaper target profile and more aggressive batching, versus a latency route. But yes, you can route by tier.

[21:10] Arjun Mehta: Got it.

[21:12] Markus Klein: Cool.

[21:14] Markus Klein: Recap: we’ll send POC plan, propose fallback matrix, you’ll send sanitized traffic sample and SLOs, and we’ll schedule kickoff.

[21:24] Dana Wu: Works.

[21:25] Sofia Ramirez: Sounds good.

[21:27] Arjun Mehta: Thanks.

[21:29] Markus Klein: Thanks all. We’ll follow up tomorrow.


(Transcript continues with light small talk and scheduling details; Fireflies truncated non-substantive section.)
